claims.text: Adding a modest amount of an additional element to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve its glass-forming ability.
The same minor alloying addition will improve the thermal stability of the resulting amorphous state.
The proposed additive concentration is on the order of a few atomic percent, exemplified as 2–5 at%.
The additive should have a large atomic-size mismatch relative to the alloy constituents.
The additive should interact strongly with phosphorus and the other alloy constituents.
The addition will increase atomic packing disorder.
The addition will disrupt medium-range order that otherwise facilitates crystallization.
Enhanced local structural disorder will increase the kinetic barrier for crystallization.
The structural disruption will suppress nucleation during cooling.
The structural disruption will retard devitrification during heating.
Relative to an otherwise comparable additive-free baseline, the modified alloy will have a higher critical casting thickness.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have a higher crystallization onset temperature, Tx.
Critical casting thickness is a proxy for glass-forming ability.
Crystallization onset temperature is a proxy for the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The beneficial effect will occur only within a narrow additive-concentration range.
Additive concentrations that are too high may form secondary phases or induce crystallinity, eliminating or reversing the benefit.
The benefit is expected under rapid-quenching conditions, whereas very slow cooling may not produce the improvement.
